  • Guardrail brittleness and offline use: Safety filters are easy to bypass and don’t apply if model weights are available offline. Once released, models can be modified to remove protections.
  • Proliferation and irreversibility: Open‑weight releases and model leaks cannot be “recalled.” Capabilities spread globally and permanently, even to jurisdictions with weak enforcement.

How a ban would reduce the threat

  • Raises the bar for attackers: With no new or more capable models, fewer turnkey tools exist to convert intent into action. Lone actors must rely on traditional skills, which are harder to acquire and apply at scale.
  • Slows capability diffusion: Banning development (especially of frontier and general-purpose models) limits the pool of models that can be repurposed for offense, and reduces the chance of irreversible open‑weight releases.
  • Buys defender time: A pause stretches the window for patching systemic weaknesses, hardening critical infrastructure, updating security tooling, and building legal frameworks before faster, more agentic AI arrives.
  • Reduces automation of the full kill chain: Without increasingly capable agents, single operators find it harder to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, lateral movement, and monetization end-to-end.
  • Limits deepfake-enabled fraud and social engineering: Fewer high‑quality generative models means fewer convincing voice/video spoofs and less mass‑customized deception that lone actors can deploy.
  • Improves attribution and deterrence: If advanced AI isn’t widely available, sophisticated attacks are more likely to be linked to well-resourced groups rather than individuals, making investigation and deterrence more feasible.
  • Curbs worst‑case tail risks: Prevents or delays scenarios where adaptive AI could assist in creating self‑modifying or fast-spreading cyber campaigns that overwhelm defenses.

Why a ban is argued to be more effective than lighter regulation

  • Enforcement simplicity: A bright-line prohibition on training and releasing new models is easier to verify than nuanced restrictions on use-cases or content, which are easy to evade.
  • Precaution under uncertainty: Given rapid capability jumps and evaluation gaps, a ban prioritizes avoiding irreversible harms over speculative benefits.
  • Nonproliferation logic: Similar to controls on nuclear materials or select pathogens, preventing the creation and spread of dual-use AI capabilities may be the only robust way to keep them out of the hands of lone actors.

Conditions needed for the ban to work

  • Coverage of compute, data, and weights: Controls on high‑end chips, model training at scale, and distribution of existing weights; penalties for retraining or fine‑tuning powerful models.
  • International coordination: To prevent displacement to permissive jurisdictions and reduce cross‑border leakage.
  • Complementary cybersecurity investments: Hardening legacy systems, improving identity verification, and strengthening incident response so that when the ban eventually lifts (or is imperfect), the ecosystem is more resilient.

Expected security benefits

  • Fewer high-impact incidents enabled by novice attackers; reduced volume and sophistication of phishing/fraud.
  • Lower probability of catastrophic, fast-moving attacks against critical infrastructure initiated by a single actor.
  • Preservation of trust in digital communications and financial transactions by limiting realistic synthetic media.
  • More manageable threat landscape where defenders’ tools and training can keep pace with adversary capability.

In short: From a cybersecurity standpoint, banning AI development is argued to shrink the attack surface created by powerful, general-purpose, easily repurposed models; raise the cost and skill required for serious attacks; and buy time to shore up defenses—especially against lone actors who would otherwise gain disproportionate power from AI.

I am here to argue for the second path. I am here to call for a ban on the development of high-capability AI systems—full stop—because the stakes are life-and-death, the timelines are short, and the consequences of getting this wrong even once could be irreversible.

Some will say a ban is too blunt. That we should regulate, not prohibit. But regulations built on trust and voluntary compliance cannot contain technologies that, once released, can be copied, leaked, and run on a laptop. You cannot roll back a model that has been downloaded a million times. You cannot negotiate with code that spreads faster than legislation can be drafted. Licensing and audits have their place, but they cannot defend us against the simplest threat of all: someone, somewhere, deciding to push a button with no regard for the consequences.

Others will warn that a ban will cost us economic growth or cede leadership to rivals. But leadership is not measured in quarterly returns; it is measured in the safety and stability we secure for our people. We did not win the nuclear age by racing to put fissile material in every garage. We won it by establishing red lines, building verification regimes, and refusing to normalize existential risk in the name of convenience. The measure of a mature society is not how fast it builds, but how wisely it chooses not to.

And let me be clear: this is not a rejection of progress. It is a recognition that progress without guardrails is not progress at all. True innovation does not leave hospitals exposed to ransomware in the middle of a pandemic. It does not open the door for one person to lock down a power grid from a basement apartment. It does not treat our children’s identities, our soldiers’ voices, and our civic trust as acceptable collateral damage.

A ban is not forever; it is for as long as it takes. It is a firewall, not a surrender. It buys us time to:

  • Build verifiable defenses that do not depend on wishful thinking.
  • Develop containment architectures that make misuse measurably harder than defense.
  • Establish enforceable international norms that treat high-capability models like hazardous materials—tracked, controlled, and never casually released.
  • Create accountability that puts liability on those who push dangerous systems into the world and profits in front of prudence.

What would a ban mean in practice? It means halting the training and release of frontier models that can be adapted for offensive cyber operations or large-scale deception. It means shutting down the pipelines that convert raw computing power into ungovernable capability. It means saying, plainly, that there are some lines we do not cross—not because we are afraid of the future, but because we want one.

We already regulate the materials that can level a city, the chemicals that can poison a water supply, the pathogens that can start a pandemic. We do this not because we distrust science, but because we understand risk. High-capability AI belongs on that list. It is compute, data, and algorithms—yes—but it is also power. And when power accumulates faster than our systems of accountability, we must intervene.

Ask yourself: if a lone actor disabled emergency services in your town, and investigators found that an off-the-shelf model had walked them through every step, would we feel that the “innovators” who shipped it had been cautious enough? If a deepfake of a national leader triggered a crisis before it could be debunked, would we wish we had moved faster? If your loved one were on the operating table when a hospital network went dark, would you accept that we prioritized convenience over caution?

We do not get infinite warnings. We get a handful of near-misses, a chorus of experts saying “slow down,” and a rapidly closing window in which the costs of decisive action are bearable. The window is open today. It will not be open long.

So let us choose courage over comfort. Let us enact a ban on the development of high-capability AI systems until we have the defensive technologies, the legal frameworks, and the international coordination to ensure that a lone actor cannot turn our own ingenuity against us. Let us lead, not by building the most dangerous tools the fastest, but by protecting the society that makes innovation meaningful in the first place.

We will be judged—by our children, by history—not on how cleverly we pushed the limits of what we could do, but on whether we had the wisdom to stop when we should. The urgent, moral, responsible choice is to ban this development now.

Not next year. Not after the next release. Now.

Thank you.

The Case for Banning AI Development: The Lone Actor Cybersecurity Threat

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

Throughout human history, societies have confronted a recurring dilemma: what do we do when a powerful technology's destructive potential outweighs its benefits? We banned biological weapons not because microbiology lacked promise, but because the catastrophic downside demanded restraint. We restricted the proliferation of nuclear materials not because nuclear science was without merit, but because the consequences of placing fissile material in the wrong hands were too terrible to permit. Today, we face the same inflection point with artificial intelligence. AI—particularly large language models, autonomous agents, and code-generation systems—is rapidly lowering the barrier to entry for catastrophic cyberattacks, placing capabilities once reserved for nation-state intelligence agencies into the hands of isolated individuals with little training and fewer scruples. The development of AI should be banned because it creates an unacceptable, perhaps civilization-threatening, risk of enabling lone actors to cause devastating and irreversible cybersecurity damage to critical infrastructure, financial systems, and democratic institutions.

I. AI as a Force Multiplier: Redefining What a Single Person Can Do

The fundamental danger of AI in the cybersecurity context is not that it creates entirely new categories of attack—it is that it democratizes attack capabilities that previously required teams of dozens of elite specialists, millions of dollars, and months or years of development.

Consider what offensive cyber operations historically required. The Stuxnet worm, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges, is widely attributed to a joint operation between the United States and Israel. Its creation demanded deep expertise in industrial control systems, multiple zero-day exploits, sophisticated evasion techniques, extensive intelligence about the target environment, and rigorous testing—resources available only to the world's most capable intelligence services. The 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack, attributed to North Korea's Lazarus Group, leveraged an NSA-developed exploit and still required state-level coordination.

AI fundamentally upends this calculus. Modern AI systems can already:

  • Discover software vulnerabilities at machine speed. Systems like those demonstrated by researchers at DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge can analyze millions of lines of code and identify exploitable weaknesses far faster than human analysts. As these models improve, they will find zero-day vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure software that human researchers might take years to discover—or might never find at all.

  • Generate exploit code from vulnerability descriptions. Large language models fine-tuned on security research can already produce working proof-of-concept exploits. A lone actor who identifies—or who instructs an AI to identify—a vulnerability in a power grid's SCADA system need not possess the programming expertise to write the attack code personally. The AI will write it for them.

  • Automate social engineering at scale. Phishing—still the most common initial attack vector for major breaches—has historically been limited by human effort. A lone actor could send hundreds of emails, perhaps thousands. An AI agent can craft individually personalized, contextually convincing phishing messages for millions of targets simultaneously, in any language, mimicking any communication style, adapting in real time to responses.

  • Coordinate complex, multi-stage attacks autonomously. Emerging AI agent frameworks allow models to plan, execute, observe results, and adapt—the core loop of sophisticated cyber operations. What once required a team of operators managing an intrusion over weeks can increasingly be managed by AI systems operating at machine speed, directed by a single individual.

The net effect is that AI compresses the resource requirements for catastrophic cyberattacks by orders of magnitude. A skilled but solitary individual—a disgruntled former employee, a radicalized extremist, a sociopathic teenager—can now aspire to mount attacks that previously required the backing of a nation-state. This is not a marginal increase in risk. It is a qualitative transformation of the threat landscape.

II. The Asymmetry Problem: Why Defense Cannot Keep Pace

Proponents of continued AI development frequently argue that AI will benefit defenders as much as attackers—that the same tools enabling offense will strengthen cybersecurity. This argument, while superficially appealing, collapses under scrutiny because of a fundamental asymmetry that has defined cybersecurity since its inception and that AI dramatically worsens.

Defenders must protect everything; attackers need only find one weakness. A nation's critical infrastructure encompasses power grids, water treatment facilities, financial networks, transportation systems, healthcare databases, telecommunications, and more. Each system contains millions of lines of code, thousands of configuration decisions, and countless potential points of failure. The defender must secure all of them. The attacker—especially an AI-augmented lone actor—needs to find and exploit one.

AI worsens this asymmetry for several reasons:

  1. Speed of exploitation versus speed of patching. When an AI system discovers a zero-day vulnerability, it can generate exploit code and launch an attack in minutes or hours. Patching a vulnerability across an entire infrastructure—especially in legacy industrial control systems that cannot be easily taken offline—takes weeks, months, or sometimes years. The attacker operates at AI speed; the defender operates at bureaucratic speed.

  2. The defender's AI must be perfect; the attacker's AI must be lucky once. An AI-powered defensive system that catches 99.9% of threats still allows one in a thousand through. Against an attacker generating thousands of novel attack vectors per hour, this is not a rounding error—it is a breach.

  3. Attackers can use AI without constraint; defenders face institutional friction. Deploying AI in defensive roles within critical infrastructure requires extensive testing, regulatory approval, integration with legacy systems, and institutional buy-in. A lone attacker, accountable to no one, can deploy cutting-edge offensive AI immediately and without hesitation.

  4. AI-generated attacks can exhibit unprecedented novelty. Machine-learning systems can produce attack patterns that bear no resemblance to historical threats, rendering signature-based detection systems—still the backbone of most cybersecurity defenses—effectively blind. The attacker using AI doesn't just move faster; they move in directions defenders have never seen.

The "AI helps defense too" argument ultimately amounts to an arms race theory—and arms races, history teaches us, are not stable. They are won by whichever side has the structural advantage. In cybersecurity, the structural advantage has always belonged to the attacker. AI doesn't level the playing field; it tilts it further.

III. Critical Infrastructure: The Stakes Are Civilizational

To understand why lone-actor cyber threats justifying banning AI are not hypothetical, one must appreciate the fragility of the infrastructure on which modern civilization depends.

Power Grids: In 2015 and 2016, Russian state hackers successfully shut down portions of Ukraine's electrical grid, leaving hundreds of thousands without power in winter. These attacks required substantial resources and expertise. AI places equivalent—or superior—capability within reach of an individual. A lone actor who successfully compromises the control systems of a major grid operator could trigger cascading failures affecting tens of millions of people. Extended power outages cause deaths—in hospitals, in homes dependent on electric heating or cooling, in water systems dependent on electric pumps. A sophisticated AI-planned attack targeting multiple grid interconnections simultaneously could produce a blackout lasting not hours but weeks, with consequences rivaling a natural disaster.

Financial Systems: Global financial networks process trillions of dollars in transactions daily. The systems underlying these transactions—SWIFT, Fedwire, automated clearinghouses—are complex, interconnected, and dependent on digital trust. A lone actor leveraging AI to compromise these systems could trigger financial panic, freeze transactions, corrupt records, or siphon assets at scale. The 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist, in which hackers stole $81 million through SWIFT, was conducted by a state-sponsored team and was partially thwarted by a typo. An AI-assisted lone actor would not make typos—and might aim for far more than $81 million.

Water and Sanitation: In 2021, an attacker accessed the systems controlling a water treatment plant in Oldsmar, Florida, and attempted to increase sodium hydroxide levels to poisonous concentrations. The attack was detected and reversed by an alert operator. AI-generated attacks that are more sophisticated, better timed, and harder to detect could succeed where the Oldsmar attacker failed—with potentially lethal consequences for entire communities.

Healthcare: Hospitals and healthcare networks are notoriously vulnerable to cyberattacks, as the wave of ransomware attacks in recent years has demonstrated. AI-assisted attacks on hospital systems during a health crisis could disable life-support systems, corrupt medical records, disrupt drug supply chains, and directly cause patient deaths.

The convergence of AI-enabled attack capabilities with the fragility of critical infrastructure creates a threat matrix in which a single motivated individual could cause damage measured not in dollars but in lives—potentially thousands or tens of thousands of lives. No previous technology has placed this magnitude of destructive power in the hands of a lone actor without requiring access to physical materials (such as fissile material or weaponized pathogens) that can be physically controlled. AI is purely informational; it can be copied, shared, and distributed with zero marginal cost. This makes it, in a meaningful sense, more dangerous and harder to control than nuclear or biological weapons.

IV. The Inadequacy of Regulation Short of a Ban

Many well-intentioned voices in the policy community argue that the risks of AI can be managed through regulation, oversight, and responsible development practices—without resorting to an outright ban. This position is dangerously naive for several reasons.

The open-source problem. Powerful AI models have already been released as open-source software, freely downloadable and modifiable by anyone. Meta's LLaMA models, Stability AI's image generators, and numerous other systems are available to any person on earth with a computer. Regulations governing how companies develop AI are irrelevant to a lone actor who has already downloaded an open-source model and is fine-tuning it on offensive security data in their basement. The horse has left the barn—but banning further development is how you stop the next, more powerful horse from being bred.

The alignment problem remains unsolved. Despite billions of dollars in research, no one has yet demonstrated a reliable method for ensuring that AI systems behave in accordance with human values and intentions. "Guardrails" built into commercial AI systems are routinely circumvented through jailbreaking techniques—many of them trivially simple. A system that refuses to generate malware when asked politely will often comply when the request is framed as a fictional scenario, a security research exercise, or a hypothetical. These are not robust safeguards; they are speed bumps on a highway.

Regulatory capture and competitive pressure. The AI industry is dominated by corporations with enormous financial incentives to continue development and deployment. These companies spend heavily on lobbying, fund sympathetic research, and employ a revolving door of government officials. History provides no example of an industry this profitable being effectively regulated against its own interests without an outright prohibition. The tobacco industry delayed regulation for decades. The fossil fuel industry has successfully weakened climate policy for half a century. The idea that AI companies will submit to regulations that meaningfully constrain their products is fantasy.

International coordination failure. Even if one nation bans or strictly regulates AI development, others will continue. This is the classic argument against unilateral action—and it is often persuasive. But in this case, the alternative is worse. A world in which every nation races to develop the most powerful AI systems, with no nation willing to stop first, is a world barreling toward catastrophe. Someone must be willing to lead. International bans on biological weapons, landmines, and cluster munitions all began with unilateral or small-coalition action that built moral authority and momentum. The same model can apply here.

The precautionary principle demands action now. We do not have the luxury of waiting for a catastrophic lone-actor AI-enabled cyberattack before acting. By the time such an attack occurs, the damage will be done—and the capabilities enabling it will have proliferated beyond recall. The precautionary principle, which holds that when an activity raises threats of serious or irreversible harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if some cause-and-effect relationships are not fully established scientifically, demands that we act before the worst-case scenario materializes. We do not wait for the bomb to detonate before deciding whether to restrict bomb-making materials.

V. The Moral Calculus: Benefits Do Not Justify Existential Risk

The most powerful objection to banning AI is that the technology offers enormous benefits: medical breakthroughs, scientific discovery, economic productivity, solutions to climate change, and more. These benefits are real and significant. But the moral calculus does not support the conclusion that they justify the risk.

Consider the following thought experiment. Suppose a pharmaceutical company developed a drug that cured a wide range of diseases but could also, with trivial modification, be converted into a nerve agent capable of killing thousands. Suppose further that the recipe for this modification was freely available and that no reliable method existed for preventing the modification. Would we permit the drug's continued manufacture on the grounds that its medical benefits were substantial? Of course not. We would ban it and seek alternative treatments.

AI is that drug. Its benefits are real but replaceable—given time, many of the same advances can be pursued through narrower, more controllable computational methods that do not create general-purpose systems capable of being weaponized. Its risks, however, are unique and irreplaceable—no other technology threatens to give every individual on earth the offensive cyber capability of a nation-state intelligence agency.

Furthermore, the distribution of benefits and risks is profoundly unjust. The benefits of AI accrue disproportionately to wealthy corporations and technologically advanced nations. The risks—particularly the risk of infrastructure attacks—fall disproportionately on ordinary people, who depend on functioning power grids, clean water, and stable financial systems and who have no say in the development decisions creating these dangers. Banning AI development is not merely prudent; it is a matter of justice.

VI. Addressing Common Objections

"You can't ban a technology." This is empirically false. Human cloning for reproduction is banned in most countries and has not occurred. Blinding laser weapons were banned before they were ever used in combat. The development of new chemical weapons has been effectively suppressed for decades. Bans on technology are imperfect, but imperfect containment is vastly preferable to no containment at all.

"Banning AI will just drive it underground." Some degree of illicit development is inevitable, just as some degree of illicit drug manufacturing persists despite prohibition. But a ban dramatically reduces the scale and capability of development. Underground AI research, deprived of the massive computational infrastructure, talent pipelines, and institutional support that currently drive progress, will advance far more slowly and produce far less capable systems than the current research ecosystem.

"Other countries will develop AI even if we don't." As addressed above, this argument proves too much—it would counsel against any arms control agreement ever. Leadership requires accepting short-term disadvantage in pursuit of long-term survival. Moreover, a nation that bans AI development and leads the international effort to restrict it gains moral authority and diplomatic leverage that can be used to build a broader coalition.

"AI is already here; banning further development is futile." Current AI systems, while dangerous, are not yet capable of the worst-case scenarios described above. But they are on a clear trajectory toward those capabilities. Banning further development now freezes progress at a point where the risks, while serious, are still manageable. Waiting until AI systems can autonomously plan and execute civilization-threatening cyberattacks before acting is like waiting until the water reaches your neck before learning to swim.

Conclusion

The development of artificial intelligence is creating a world in which a single disaffected individual, working alone in a room with a laptop, can credibly threaten the critical infrastructure on which millions of lives depend. This is not science fiction; it is the logical and rapidly approaching consequence of current technological trajectories. The cybersecurity asymmetry that has always favored attackers is being supercharged by AI to a degree that no defensive measure can reliably counter. The stakes—blackouts, financial collapse, poisoned water supplies, hospital shutdowns, mass casualties—are too high to be managed through half-measures, voluntary guidelines, or regulations that the industry will resist and lone actors will ignore.

We ban technologies when their capacity for catastrophic misuse exceeds our capacity to control them. We did it with biological weapons. We did it with certain classes of nuclear technology. We must now do it with artificial intelligence. The benefits of AI, however impressive, do not justify accepting a world in which any individual can hold civilization hostage. The time to act is now—before the attack we failed to prevent forces us to confront the ban we failed to enact.

The only responsible path forward is a comprehensive, internationally coordinated ban on the development of advanced AI systems, coupled with a managed wind-down of existing capabilities and a redirection of resources toward safer, narrower computational tools that do not place the keys to societal destruction in every pair of hands on earth. Our survival may depend on our willingness to say: this far, and no further.
